title: Making it up
hook: missed days are made up later, or a poor person fed for each day if unable

segments.voice: Yesterday, rukhsah, the allowance, and your line: the fast bends. The sick, the traveler, the pregnant and nursing, and more. Did you give someone the benefit of a reason you couldn't see? Day one thousand one hundred eight.

It's Sha'ban, the month before Ramadan, and in a house in Medina a woman is keeping fasts that belong to last Ramadan. She isn't adding anything extra. She's paying back. The woman is Aisha, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and she says it herself in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari: she would have days of Ramadan to make up, and she couldn't make them up until the month of Sha'ban. Months could pass with that small debt waiting. Today's word is the name for paying it.
screen: `THE MONTH BEFORE RAMADAN.` → `AISHA, KEEPING OLD FASTS.` → `PAYING BACK.`

segments.voice: The word is qada'. In the law, it means making up an act of worship after its time has passed. First, it comes straight from the verse we met yesterday. The sick and the traveler fast, in Pickthall's words, "(the same) number of other days." And the next verse gives a reason: Allah desires ease, and desires "that ye should complete the period." So the allowance doesn't erase the days. It moves them. The month is still completed, just not all inside the month. Second, Aisha shows the timing can be loose. She made up her days in Sha'ban, the month just before the next Ramadan. Scholars take from this that the make-up days can wait, though not past the next Ramadan. Schools differ on what's owed if someone lets them slide past that without a reason. Third, the days don't have to be in a row. The verse says only other days, and scholars read that as allowing them to be spread out: a Monday here, a Thursday there, a quiet Saturday in winter when the days are short. And yesterday's report from Aisha in Sahih Muslim fits here too: women make up the fasts missed during their periods. Fourth, there's one more case, and tomorrow is about it. Some people will never be able to make the days up: the very old, the permanently ill. For them, the verse has another answer, and it involves feeding someone. Away from the fast, qada' is a way of thinking about any commitment you couldn't keep on time. Not canceled. Not a failure. Owed, and waiting for its day.
screen: `QADA': MAKING IT UP LATER.` · `THE DAYS MOVE, THEY DON'T VANISH.` · `AISHA, IN SHA'BAN.` · `SPREAD OUT, ONE BY ONE.` · then, large: `THAT YE SHOULD COMPLETE THE PERIOD.`

segments.voice: The practice: plan any make-up days. Let your shoulders drop, and breathe. If you fast and owe days, see a calendar in your mind and quietly place them: which weeks, which days, before the next Ramadan. If you don't, find one thing you meant to do and didn't: a call you owe, a thank-you note, a visit you postponed. Don't scold yourself. Just give it a date. Hold that date for the rest of these two minutes. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make it easy. The bell holds the time.
Qada'. Making up a missed act of worship after its time; here, fasting the missed days of Ramadan later in the year. Today's word.
Your line: made up later. Today, put one postponed promise on an actual calendar, with a day and a time. Day one thousand one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Muslims who miss Ramadan fasts for illness, travel, pregnancy, nursing or menstruation fast the same number of days later in the year, before the next Ramadan, together or spread out.

what a scholar hears: qada', from 2:184–185, with Aisha's Sha'ban report setting how long it may wait.
